preamble: Depalatalization of [ʃ] to [s] involves the movement of the articulation from the post-alveolar to the alveolar region. In Samic, Proto-Uralic *š merged completely with *s (*iša 'skin' > Proto-Samic *ësē), while Finnic took the opposite route to h. In Polish dialects with mazurzenie (Masovia, Masuria, most of Lesser Poland, parts of Silesia), the older soft palato-alveolar /ʃ/ (sz) merged with /s/ as the series lost its palatalization, while the standard language and the other dialects turned it into retroflex /ʂ/. Wikipedia dates this depalatalization to around the 16th century and places the origin of mazurzenie in the Masovian dialect between the 14th and 16th centuries. For example, sześć 'six' is mazurating [sɛɕt͡ɕ] against standard [ʂɛɕt͡ɕ], and szyty 'sewn' sounds like syty 'full' [sɨtɨ]. Wikipedia (Mazuration, after Dejna, Kuraszkiewicz and Rospond) says that in these dialects "the postalveolar sibilants merged completely with the dentialveolars", and Koneczna derives the merger directly from the depalatalization. In Kuryłowicz's account the archaic dialects, trying to adopt the neighbours' new retroflex /ʂ ʐ/, replaced them with the /s z/ they already had. Old Polish had soft palato-alveolars (/t͡ʃʲ ʃʲ ʒʲ d͡ʒʲ/ in Wiktionary's transcription); they are filed here under the plain symbols.

examples.note: Proto-Baltic turned PIE *ḱ into *ś, 'later merged into *š' (Wikipedia, Proto-Baltic language); Latvian made this *š into s, while Lithuanian keeps š (šimtas).
Smoczyński (1982: 227), as excerpted in the Vilnius University etymological database: Latvian suns < *sunis, which with Lithuanian šuõ and Old Prussian sunis continues Baltic *šu̯ōn- < PIE *k̑u̯ōn-.
